country.evidence_source: [/page/3/Text/19] Although a substantial body of research has highlighted that LS is an important factor leading to positive developmental outcomes among adolescents, there has been a scarcity of research examining the effects of LS on DBs during adolescence. The aim of the current study was to extend the positive psychology literature by investing the long-term effects of LS on DBs by comparing the bidirectional model between LS and DBs over four years. In addition, this study explored the interactive effects of initial LS on the associations between initial DBs and later DBs among Korean adolescents. [/page/3/Text/19] Contrary to our expectation, the trajectories of DBs among Korean adolescents showed different patterns to those seen among Western adolescents. While DBs among Western adolescents typically increased during preadolescence and peaked in mid- to late adolescence (15- to 17-years-old) before then decreasing (Farrington, 1986; Loeber et al., 1989), DBs among Korean adolescents decreased in mid-adolescence (14- to 16-years-old) and then increased thereafter in this study. This result was not consistent with previous findings that documented Asian adolescents in Western countries (Le and Stockdale, 2011; Vazsonyi and Keiley, 2007). We speculated that this finding might be due to the measures of DBs used in the current study, which included some status offense items. While the examples of DBs in the study by Le and Stockdale (2011) consisted of carrying a hand gun and selling or supplying drugs such as marijuana, examples of DBs in this study included smoking, drinking alcohol, having sex, and running away from home. These behaviors are illegal for adolescents, but not for adults. According to a recent online survey of Korean adolescents' health status, the smoking and drinking rates of middle school students were 3.3% and 7.4%, respectively, whereas those of high school students were 11.4% and 24.7%, respectively, in Korea (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2015). Given that the increase in DBs occurred when the participating adolescents were high school students, these items might contribute to the increase of DBs identified in the current study. Thus, future research studies should examine the same measures of DBs among adolescents in different cultures in order to compare the trajectories of DBs across cultures.
